domain: Monitoring, Logging, Analysis, Remediation, and Performance Optimization
stem: A CloudOps team wants a single CloudWatch alarm that only enters ALARM state when both an ALB 5xx-error alarm and at least two of three per-instance CPU alarms are simultaneously in ALARM, so the on-call engineer is paged only for a real correlated incident instead of every transient per-instance blip. The individual alarms must keep evaluating and recording their own history for diagnostics. Which TWO statements about meeting this requirement with a composite alarm are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: A composite alarm combines other alarms using an alarm rule expression built from AND, OR, and NOT operators over ALARM() functions referencing each underlying alarm.
Creating a composite alarm automatically deletes the underlying alarms it references, so only the composite alarm remains for diagnostics.
The underlying alarms keep evaluating independently and retain their own state history after being referenced by a composite alarm.
A composite alarm can reference at most two underlying alarms and cannot express a rule like at least two of three.
Composite alarms evaluate on a fixed one-minute period regardless of the underlying alarms, so every per-instance alarm must be changed to match.
explanation: A composite alarm is built from an alarm rule expression that combines other alarms' ALARM() states with AND, OR, and NOT, so it can express exactly a rule like the 5xx alarm AND at least two of the three CPU alarms. The underlying alarms keep evaluating and recording their own history unchanged, so they stay useful for diagnostics and dashboards. Creating a composite alarm does not delete or modify the alarms it references. A composite alarm can reference many underlying alarms, not just two, which is exactly what makes at-least-two-of-three expressions possible. A composite alarm has no fixed one-minute evaluation period of its own; it reacts to the state of the alarms in its rule.

domain: Monitoring, Logging, Analysis, Remediation, and Performance Optimization
stem: A support engineer must find the five endpoints that returned the most HTTP 500 responses across a fleet of application servers in the last hour, using the structured JSON access logs already stored in a CloudWatch Logs log group. Which approach requires the LEAST setup?
options: Run a CloudWatch Logs Insights query that parses the log fields, filters on status 500, and uses stats count() by endpoint with a sort and limit.
Export the log group to Amazon S3, load it into Amazon Athena with an AWS Glue crawler, and run a SQL GROUP BY query.
Create a separate CloudWatch Logs metric filter for every possible endpoint value, then compare each metric's alarm history.
Connect to each application server with Session Manager and grep the local log file on every instance by hand.
explanation: CloudWatch Logs Insights queries structured or unstructured log data directly with fields, filter, and stats, so a single ad hoc query returns the top five endpoints with no extra infrastructure. Exporting to S3 and standing up a Glue crawler plus Athena is a much heavier pipeline for a one-time ranking. A metric filter per endpoint requires knowing every endpoint value in advance and does not produce a ranked top-N. Grepping each server manually over Session Manager does not scale across a fleet and is not ad hoc query capable.

domain: Monitoring, Logging, Analysis, Remediation, and Performance Optimization
stem: An application team wants to publish a custom business metric, checkout_latency_ms, from application code running on ECS tasks, using the same structured JSON log line the application already writes to stdout, and without adding a separate CloudWatch PutMetricData API call in the request path. Which approach BEST meets this need?
options: Call the CloudWatch PutMetricData API directly from the checkout code on every request.
Write the metric using the CloudWatch embedded metric format in the existing structured log line, and let the CloudWatch agent or Lambda extension extract it into a CloudWatch metric automatically.
Store the latency value only in a DynamoDB table and build a nightly batch job to compute an average.
Increase the CloudWatch Logs retention period so the value can be found later by scanning the raw logs.
explanation: The CloudWatch embedded metric format (EMF) lets an application emit metrics as part of the structured log line it already writes; the CloudWatch agent or the Lambda extension parses the EMF metadata block and creates a real CloudWatch metric with no direct API call in the hot path. Calling PutMetricData directly is exactly the extra call the team wants to avoid. Writing to DynamoDB and batching a nightly average does not create a CloudWatch metric available for real-time alarms or dashboards. Longer log retention only keeps raw logs around longer; it does not create a metric.

domain: Monitoring, Logging, Analysis, Remediation, and Performance Optimization
stem: A CloudOps team wants to know within minutes when a customer-facing login page becomes unreachable or its response time degrades, even during low-traffic overnight hours when real user requests are too sparse to produce a meaningful CloudWatch alarm from actual traffic metrics. Which approach BEST provides this proactive signal?
options: Enable AWS X-Ray tracing on the login service and review the collected traces the next business day.
Create a CloudWatch Logs metric filter on the login service's error logs.
Create a CloudWatch Synthetics canary that runs a scripted login flow on a fixed schedule from outside the account and alarms on failures or elevated duration.
Enable Amazon GuardDuty and create a CloudWatch alarm on any HIGH severity finding.
explanation: A CloudWatch Synthetics canary runs a scripted flow on a schedule regardless of real user traffic, so it produces a steady, proactive availability and latency signal even overnight. Reviewing X-Ray traces the next business day is reactive, not a near-real-time signal. A metric filter on error logs still depends on real requests occurring to generate log lines, which is exactly what's sparse overnight. GuardDuty detects security threats, not login-page availability or latency, so it would not surface this kind of degradation.

domain: Monitoring, Logging, Analysis, Remediation, and Performance Optimization
stem: An application writes the string OutOfMemoryError to its CloudWatch Logs log group whenever a worker process crashes, but no CloudWatch metric tracks this event today. The team wants an alarm that notifies an SNS topic within a few minutes of the tenth occurrence in a 5-minute window, without changing the application code. Which combination of steps accomplishes this?
options: Enable CloudWatch cross-account observability so the log data streams to a separate monitoring account.
Create an AWS Config rule that evaluates the log group's retention setting and reports noncompliant resources.
Turn on CloudWatch Application Insights for the log group and wait for its automated dashboard to appear.

Create a CloudWatch Logs metric filter matching the pattern OutOfMemoryError, publish it as a custom metric, then create a CloudWatch alarm on that metric with a threshold of 10 over a 5-minute period and an SNS alarm action.
explanation: A CloudWatch Logs metric filter turns a matching log pattern into a custom metric with no code change, and a standard CloudWatch alarm on that metric with an SNS action delivers the threshold-based notification the team wants. Cross-account observability changes where data can be viewed, not whether an alarm fires on a log pattern. An AWS Config rule evaluates resource configuration, such as retention settings, not log content. Application Insights builds an automated dashboard and some baseline alarms for a detected stack, but it does not create a targeted alarm on a specific custom error string on demand.

domain: Monitoring, Logging, Analysis, Remediation, and Performance Optimization
stem: A security-conscious CloudOps team wants any Amazon EC2 instance that transitions to the running state without a required CostCenter tag to be automatically stopped within seconds, with no human review step and no scheduled polling job. Which design BEST meets this requirement?
options: Create an EventBridge rule that matches the EC2 instance state-change event for the running state, and target a Lambda function that checks the instance's tags and stops it if CostCenter is missing.
Schedule an AWS Config rule evaluation to run once every 24 hours and stop noncompliant instances at the next evaluation.
Create a CloudWatch alarm on the EC2 StatusCheckFailed metric and configure an EC2 action to stop the instance.
Enable AWS Trusted Advisor's cost checks and review the weekly email report for untagged instances.
explanation: EC2 publishes an instance state-change event the moment an instance reaches running, so an EventBridge rule targeting a Lambda function reacts within seconds with no polling and no person in the loop. A daily AWS Config evaluation is polling and can leave a noncompliant instance running for up to 24 hours. A StatusCheckFailed alarm reacts to instance health failures, not tag compliance, so it would never fire for a missing tag. Trusted Advisor's weekly email is a manual, delayed report, not an automated near-real-time control.

domain: Monitoring, Logging, Analysis, Remediation, and Performance Optimization
stem: A CloudWatch alarm enters ALARM state when a critical Windows service stops responding on a fleet of managed EC2 instances. The team wants this alarm to trigger a self-healing AWS Systems Manager Automation runbook that restarts the service, without writing and maintaining a Lambda function whose only job is to call the SSM StartAutomationExecution API. Which approach BEST meets this requirement?
options: Configure the alarm to publish to an SNS topic, and have an on-call engineer manually run the runbook from the Systems Manager console when paged.

Create an EventBridge rule that matches the CloudWatch alarm's state-change event and specifies an AWS Systems Manager Automation runbook directly as the rule's target, passing the instance ID as input.
Add a CloudWatch alarm action that invokes AWS Trusted Advisor to flag the instance for review the next business day.
Grant the alarm's default service role the ssm:StartAutomationExecution permission, since a CloudWatch alarm action can call any AWS API directly.
explanation: EventBridge can target an AWS Systems Manager Automation runbook directly from a rule, so a rule matching the CloudWatch alarm state-change event can start the runbook with no Lambda function in between. Paging a human to run the runbook manually reintroduces the delay and human step the team wants to remove. Trusted Advisor has no alarm-action integration and would not restart anything. CloudWatch alarm actions are limited to a fixed set of native action types (SNS, Auto Scaling, EC2, and SSM OpsItem or Incident Manager); they cannot be granted a role to call an arbitrary API.

domain: Monitoring, Logging, Analysis, Remediation, and Performance Optimization
stem: A CloudOps team monitors request latency for a service whose normal traffic pattern varies predictably by time of day and day of week: busy at lunch, quiet overnight, and heavier on weekdays. A single static latency threshold either misses real degradations during quiet hours or pages the on-call engineer constantly during expected peak hours. Which CloudWatch capability BEST fits this metric?
options: Configure a composite alarm that requires two static-threshold alarms to both be in ALARM before paging.
Increase the alarm's evaluation period to 24 hours so daily peaks are averaged out.
Enable CloudWatch anomaly detection on the metric so it models expected values from historical data and builds a dynamic band, then alarm when the metric falls outside that band.
Switch the metric to a one-second high-resolution metric so more data points are collected per hour.
explanation: CloudWatch anomaly detection learns the metric's historical pattern, including time-of-day and day-of-week seasonality, and creates a dynamic expected-value band, so an alarm on it reacts to genuine deviations instead of a fixed number. A composite alarm of two static thresholds still relies on static thresholds and does not model the daily pattern. Averaging over a 24-hour evaluation period hides real short-lived degradations rather than detecting them. Raising the metric's resolution changes how many data points are collected, not whether the threshold accounts for expected variation.

domain: Monitoring, Logging, Analysis, Remediation, and Performance Optimization
stem: An operations team runs a multi-tenant API on API Gateway and Lambda. After a deployment, the overall 5xx error rate rises on a shared CloudWatch metric, but the team cannot tell which of thousands of tenant API keys is responsible without scanning every log stream by hand. The application already ships structured JSON access logs, including a tenant_id field, to a CloudWatch Logs log group. Which TWO statements about using CloudWatch Contributor Insights to find the top contributors are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: Contributor Insights requires migrating the log group's data into an Amazon OpenSearch Service domain before it can rank contributors.

Contributor Insights runs a rule against the log group's structured fields, such as tenant_id, and produces a time series ranking the top contributors, without the team writing a Logs Insights query by hand.
Contributor Insights only supports AWS-provided rules for VPC Flow Logs and DynamoDB metrics and cannot define a custom rule against an application's own log fields.
A Contributor Insights report can be added to a CloudWatch dashboard as a graph, and its computed values can also be retrieved as data points through the GetInsightRuleReport API.
Enabling Contributor Insights on a log group deletes the raw log events once they are summarized, retaining only the aggregated ranking.
explanation: Contributor Insights rules operate directly on a log group's structured log fields to produce a ranked, time-series view of top contributors, such as tenant_id, with no separate query written by the team. That ranking can be graphed on a CloudWatch dashboard and pulled programmatically with GetInsightRuleReport. It does not require moving data into OpenSearch Service; it reads the log group in place. AWS provides some built-in rules for services like VPC Flow Logs and DynamoDB, but custom rules against an application's own fields are fully supported. Enabling Contributor Insights does not delete or alter the underlying raw log events.

domain: Monitoring, Logging, Analysis, Remediation, and Performance Optimization
stem: A checkout workflow calls four microservices in sequence: cart, pricing, inventory, and payment. End users report the checkout is slow, but the team does not know which of the four services, or which downstream call within a service, is responsible for the added latency. Which AWS service BEST helps pinpoint the specific call and its latency contribution within the request chain?
options: Amazon CloudWatch Contributor Insights, to rank which customer accounts issue the most checkout requests.
AWS Config, to check whether each microservice's infrastructure matches a desired-state rule.
Amazon Inspector, to scan each service's container image for software vulnerabilities.
AWS X-Ray, to trace the request across all four services and view a service map with per-segment latency breakdown.
explanation: AWS X-Ray traces a single request as it moves through every service, building a service map with per-segment latency so the slow call is directly visible. Contributor Insights ranks contributors to a metric or log field, such as top accounts, but does not trace a single request's path or per-call latency. AWS Config evaluates resource configuration against rules, not runtime request latency. Amazon Inspector scans for vulnerabilities, not performance bottlenecks.

domain: Monitoring, Logging, Analysis, Remediation, and Performance Optimization
stem: An Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL instance shows high CPU utilization in CloudWatch, but the team cannot tell which specific SQL statements or wait events are driving the load. Which AWS capability gives a database-level view of top SQL statements and wait states without installing any agent on the database?
options: Amazon RDS Performance Insights, which visualizes database load and lets the team drill down to top SQL statements and wait events.
CloudWatch Logs metric filters on the general query log, counting each unique query string.
AWS Trusted Advisor's cost-optimization checks for the RDS instance.
Amazon Inspector network reachability findings for the RDS instance's security group.
explanation: RDS Performance Insights is built into the managed RDS engine and visualizes database load broken down by top SQL statements, waits, hosts, and users, with no agent to install. A metric filter on the general query log can count query occurrences but does not classify wait events or database load, and requires the general query log to be enabled and parsed. Trusted Advisor's cost checks address spend, not database load. Inspector's network reachability findings check security group exposure, not query performance.

domain: Monitoring, Logging, Analysis, Remediation, and Performance Optimization
stem: A CloudOps team wants ongoing, data-driven right-sizing recommendations for over-provisioned EC2 instances, EBS volumes, and Auto Scaling groups, based on utilization history, without manually building and maintaining CloudWatch dashboards and thresholds for every resource. Which AWS service BEST fits this need?
options: AWS Budgets, configured with a monthly cost threshold and an alert action.
AWS Compute Optimizer, which analyzes CloudWatch utilization metrics and recommends optimal instance types, EBS volume configurations, and Auto Scaling group sizes.
Amazon CloudWatch Application Insights, which builds dashboards and alarms for a detected application stack.
The AWS Well-Architected Tool, filling out the Cost Optimization pillar questionnaire manually each quarter.
explanation: AWS Compute Optimizer continuously analyzes CloudWatch utilization history and produces specific rightsizing recommendations for EC2, EBS, and Auto Scaling groups with no dashboards to build. AWS Budgets alerts on spend thresholds; it does not recommend resource sizing. Application Insights focuses on automated health monitoring and alarms for a detected stack, not rightsizing guidance. The Well-Architected Tool is a manual, periodic self-assessment questionnaire, not a continuous, data-driven recommendation engine.

domain: Monitoring, Logging, Analysis, Remediation, and Performance Optimization
stem: A company runs workloads across 12 AWS accounts organized under AWS Organizations. The CloudOps team wants engineers in a single central monitoring account to search CloudWatch Logs, view metrics, and see traces originating in any of the 12 accounts from one CloudWatch console, without copying or duplicating the underlying log and metric data into the central account. Which capability BEST meets this requirement?
options: Configure cross-account IAM roles and require each engineer to switch roles into every source account one at a time to view its own CloudWatch console.
Set up CloudWatch Logs subscription filters that stream every source account's logs into Kinesis Data Streams and land them in the central account's own log groups.

Enable CloudWatch cross-account observability, designating the 12 accounts as monitoring account sources and the central account as the monitoring account, to view their metrics, logs, and traces directly from its console.
Turn on AWS Config aggregation so the central account receives a copy of each account's Config compliance findings.
explanation: CloudWatch cross-account observability lets a designated monitoring account query metrics, logs, and traces from linked source accounts directly, in place, from one console, with no data duplication. Switching IAM roles into each account one at a time works but never presents a single unified console view. Streaming logs into the central account's own log groups via subscription filters is exactly the kind of copying the requirement rules out. AWS Config aggregation centralizes compliance findings, not CloudWatch metrics, logs, or traces, and it also works by replicating data into the aggregator.

domain: Monitoring, Logging, Analysis, Remediation, and Performance Optimization
stem: A CloudOps team wants to be notified automatically, inside their existing incident-management pipeline, whenever AWS Health reports a scheduled maintenance event or service issue affecting a specific EC2 instance or RDS database the team owns, instead of relying on someone to check the Personal Health Dashboard manually. Which approach BEST meets this requirement?
options: Subscribe to the public AWS Service Health Dashboard RSS feed, which lists account-specific events affecting the team's resources.
Create a daily scheduled Lambda function that calls the EC2 DescribeInstances API and compares instance status checks against a hardcoded list.
Grant the team's IAM users read access to AWS Trusted Advisor checks and review the fault-tolerance category weekly.
Create an EventBridge rule that matches AWS Health events for the team's affected resources and targets an SNS topic or the existing incident-management integration.
explanation: AWS Health publishes events to EventBridge, so a rule matching those events can route account- and resource-specific maintenance and issue notifications straight into an existing incident-management pipeline with no manual checking. The public Service Health Dashboard RSS feed covers general service status, not account-specific, resource-level events. A custom Lambda function polling DescribeInstances only sees instance status checks, not the broader set of AWS Health events like scheduled maintenance. Trusted Advisor's fault-tolerance checks review configuration best practices, not live AWS Health service events.

stem: A company runs EC2 instances, RDS databases, and EFS file systems and currently backs up each service with its own separate schedule and retention setting, which makes it hard to prove a consistent recovery point objective across the whole application. The team wants one policy that defines schedule, retention, and lifecycle (including transition to cold storage) and applies it across all three resource types from a single place. Which AWS capability BEST meets this need?
options: Configure RDS automated backups, an EC2 Data Lifecycle Manager policy, and an EFS lifecycle management policy separately, then manually confirm their schedules stay aligned.
Create a single AWS Backup plan with one backup rule that assigns EC2, RDS, and EFS resources by tag, defining schedule, retention, and cold-storage transition centrally.
Write a scheduled Lambda function that calls each service's native snapshot or backup API on a timer and stores every result in one S3 bucket.
Enable AWS Config to record configuration changes for EC2, RDS, and EFS, and treat the configuration history as the backup.
explanation: AWS Backup centralizes backup policy across supported services, including EC2, RDS, and EFS, into a single backup plan with one rule for schedule, retention, and lifecycle transitions, and it assigns resources by tag so new resources are covered automatically. Managing each service's native backup feature separately keeps the inconsistency problem the team is trying to remove. A custom Lambda scheduler reinvents backup orchestration that AWS Backup already provides, with more code to maintain. AWS Config records configuration state for compliance and drift detection; it is not a backup or restore mechanism.

stem: A regulated company must retain backups of its production database for seven years and prove to auditors that, once created, no one, including account administrators, can shorten the retention period or delete a recovery point before it expires. The company also wants a copy of every backup stored in a second AWS Region in case the primary Region becomes unavailable. Which TWO AWS Backup capabilities together satisfy these requirements? (Select TWO.)
options: AWS Backup Vault Lock, which can be applied in compliance mode so retention periods can only be extended, never shortened, and recovery points cannot be deleted before they expire, even by the root user.
A cross-Region copy rule on the backup plan, which automatically copies each recovery point to a backup vault in a second Region on the same schedule.
Increasing the backup plan's backup window duration, which extends how long a backup job is allowed to run before AWS Backup marks it as failed.
Turning on S3 Intelligent-Tiering for the backup vault, which automatically enforces the seven-year retention policy on stored recovery points.
Enabling continuous backup for the database, which replaces the need for a defined retention period entirely.
explanation: AWS Backup Vault Lock in compliance mode makes retention immutable and prevents early deletion, satisfying the audit requirement, and a cross-Region copy rule on the backup plan automatically places a recovery point copy in a second Region. Extending the backup window only changes how long a job may run before being marked failed; it has nothing to do with retention or Region redundancy. S3 Intelligent-Tiering manages storage class transitions for cost, not retention enforcement, and it does not apply to AWS Backup vaults. Continuous backup enables point-in-time recovery for supported services but does not remove the need for, or replace, a defined retention policy.

stem: An RDS for MySQL database supports a critical order-processing application. The team needs the database to automatically fail over to a standby with no data loss and no manual DNS change if the primary instance or its Availability Zone becomes unavailable, and the standby is not used to offload read traffic. Which RDS deployment option BEST meets this requirement?
options: A Multi-AZ deployment, which synchronously replicates to a standby in a second Availability Zone and automatically fails over, updating the existing DB endpoint to point at the new primary.
One or more Read Replicas in the same Region, which asynchronously replicate from the primary and can be manually promoted if the primary fails.
A read replica in a second AWS Region, promoted manually during a Regional outage.
A single-AZ instance with automated backups enabled, restored to a new instance if the primary fails.
explanation: RDS Multi-AZ keeps a synchronously replicated standby in a different Availability Zone and performs automatic failover, re-pointing the same endpoint with no data loss and no manual DNS change, exactly matching the requirement. Read Replicas replicate asynchronously (so some data loss is possible on failover) and require a manual promotion step, and their normal purpose is to offload reads, not to provide automatic failover. A cross-Region read replica adds latency and still requires a manual promotion, so it does not meet the automatic, no-manual-step requirement. Restoring a single-AZ instance from backup after failure takes materially longer and loses any data since the last backup.

stem: An analytics application runs heavy reporting queries against a production RDS database, and those queries are starting to compete with transactional traffic for compute and I/O. Separately, the team wants an option they can promote to a standalone, writable database within the same Region during an emergency. Which RDS feature addresses BOTH needs?
options: Enable RDS Multi-AZ, and route the reporting queries to the standby instance.
Create one or more RDS Read Replicas, route the reporting queries to a replica, and promote a replica to a standalone instance if needed.
Increase the primary instance's storage IOPS and run the reporting queries directly against production during off-peak hours.
Enable RDS Performance Insights and use it to throttle the reporting queries automatically.
explanation: RDS Read Replicas serve read-only traffic asynchronously from the primary, offloading reporting queries from production, and a replica can be promoted to a standalone, writable instance, giving the emergency option the team wants. A Multi-AZ standby is not accessible for read traffic in single-AZ-standby deployments and exists purely for failover, not read offload. Raising IOPS and running reports against production still contends with transactional traffic; it does not offload the load. Performance Insights is an observability tool for database load; it has no throttling or workload-routing capability.

stem: A company runs an Aurora MySQL database and wants a disaster recovery target in a second AWS Region with typical replication lag under one second and a documented recovery time objective in the double-digit seconds if the primary Region fails, without managing custom replication tooling. Which approach BEST meets this requirement?
options: Create an Aurora Global Database with the primary cluster's Region and a secondary Region, and promote the secondary cluster during a Regional disruption.
Take a manual RDS snapshot every hour and copy it to the second Region using the RDS console.
Configure an RDS Read Replica in the second Region and promote it, expecting several minutes of replication lag under normal load.
Enable RDS Multi-AZ within the primary Region only, since Multi-AZ already protects against a full Regional failure.
explanation: Aurora Global Database uses dedicated, storage-level replication to a secondary Region with typical lag under one second and a fast, documented promotion path, purpose-built for cross-Region DR with low RPO and RTO. Hourly manual snapshot copies leave up to an hour of data loss exposure and a slow manual recovery process. A standard cross-Region Read Replica typically has higher replication lag than a Global Database's dedicated replication path and still requires manual promotion. Multi-AZ protects against an Availability Zone failure within one Region; it provides no protection if the entire Region is unavailable.

stem: A gaming company operates a DynamoDB table for player profiles that must accept both reads and writes with low latency from application servers in three AWS Regions simultaneously, with changes made in any Region propagating to the others. Which DynamoDB capability BEST meets this requirement?
options: DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX), deployed independently in each of the three Regions in front of a single-Region table.
DynamoDB Global Tables, configured as a multi-Region, multi-active table that replicates writes made in any Region to the others.
A DynamoDB Stream in the primary Region, consumed by a Lambda function in each other Region that writes to a local table copy.
On-demand backups of the table, restored into a new table in each additional Region on a nightly schedule.
explanation: DynamoDB Global Tables provide a fully managed, multi-Region, multi-active table where writes accepted in any replica Region propagate to the others, giving low-latency local reads and writes everywhere. DAX is a caching layer in front of a table in one Region; deploying it in three Regions does not make writes in one Region visible in another. A custom DynamoDB Streams-and-Lambda pipeline reimplements what Global Tables already provides, with more code and higher operational risk. Nightly backup restores are batch and stale by up to a day; they do not give live, low-latency multi-Region reads and writes.

stem: A company stores critical compliance documents in a single S3 bucket in one Region. The team wants object-level durability against an entire Region becoming unavailable, plus the ability to recover a previous version of an object if it is accidentally overwritten. Which combination of S3 features BEST meets this requirement?
options: Enable S3 Versioning alone, since versioning already stores every object copy in a second Region automatically.
Enable S3 Cross-Region Replication to a bucket in a second Region, and enable S3 Versioning on both the source and destination buckets.
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration, which mirrors every object to edge locations worldwide for durability.
Configure a single lifecycle rule that transitions objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive after 30 days.
explanation: S3 Cross-Region Replication copies objects to a bucket in a second Region for Regional redundancy, and S3 Versioning, which CRR requires on both buckets, preserves prior versions so an accidental overwrite can be rolled back. Versioning alone keeps multiple versions within the same bucket and Region; it does not copy data to another Region. Transfer Acceleration speeds uploads over long distances using CloudFront edge locations; it does not replicate objects for durability. A lifecycle rule to Glacier Deep Archive only changes storage class over time within the same bucket; it neither protects against a Regional outage nor preserves prior versions.

stem: A CloudOps team manages hundreds of EBS volumes across many EC2 instances and wants automated, policy-driven snapshots on a consistent schedule with automatic retention and cross-Region copy, without writing a custom scheduler. Which AWS capability BEST meets this need?
options: Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager (DLM), which creates policies that automate the creation, retention, and cross-Region copy of EBS snapshots on a schedule.
Amazon Inspector, configured to take an EBS snapshot whenever it reports a new vulnerability finding.
AWS Trusted Advisor's fault-tolerance check, which automatically snapshots any volume it flags as unprotected.
An EC2 instance user-data script that runs the CreateSnapshot API in a loop every night.
explanation: Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager lets a team define a policy, by tag, for scheduled snapshot creation, retention, and cross-Region copy, with no custom scheduler to build. Amazon Inspector reports vulnerability findings; it has no snapshot-creation capability. Trusted Advisor's fault-tolerance check only reports a finding; it does not take any automated remediation action like creating a snapshot. A user-data script calling CreateSnapshot in a loop is exactly the custom scheduler the team wants to avoid building and maintaining.

stem: A team runs a Valkey-compatible ElastiCache replication group backing a session store. They need the cluster to detect a failed primary node and automatically promote a read replica to primary within seconds, with the endpoint updated automatically, and with no application code change during the failover. Which configuration BEST meets this requirement?
options: Configure the application to catch connection errors and manually issue a failover command to the ElastiCache API.
Add more read replicas to the replication group, since a larger replica count alone triggers automatic promotion on primary failure.
Enable at-rest encryption on the replication group, since encrypted replication groups fail over automatically by default.
Enable Multi-AZ with automatic failover on the ElastiCache replication group.
explanation: ElastiCache Multi-AZ with automatic failover monitors the primary node's health and automatically promotes a replica if the primary fails, updating the cluster's endpoint with no application change required. Requiring the application to catch errors and call a failover API manually is exactly the manual intervention the requirement rules out. Adding more replicas improves read capacity and redundancy but does not by itself enable automatic failover; that requires the Multi-AZ setting. At-rest encryption protects stored data; it has no relationship to failover behavior.

stem: An Auto Scaling group serves traffic through an Application Load Balancer. An instance in the group is passing its EC2 system status checks but the application process on it has stopped responding to the load balancer's health check path. Today the Auto Scaling group only uses the default health check type, so it has not replaced the instance. Which change makes the Auto Scaling group replace this specific instance?
options: Increase the Auto Scaling group's minimum capacity so a new instance launches alongside the unhealthy one.
Enable cross-zone load balancing on the Application Load Balancer, which automatically deregisters unhealthy targets.
Change the Auto Scaling group's health check type to ELB, so instance health also reflects the load balancer's target health check, not just the EC2 status check.
Reduce the Auto Scaling group's cooldown period so scaling activities occur more frequently.
explanation: By default, an Auto Scaling group only considers EC2 status checks, which this instance is passing. Setting the group's health check type to ELB makes it also honor the load balancer's target health check, so an instance failing application-level health checks gets marked unhealthy and replaced. Increasing minimum capacity adds instances but does not detect or replace the specific failing one. Cross-zone load balancing distributes traffic evenly across targets in all enabled Availability Zones; it does not change how Auto Scaling determines instance health. Reducing the cooldown period changes how soon new scaling activities can start; it does not add ELB health check awareness.

stem: A company's DR budget analysis shows they can accept an RTO of a few hours and want to keep DR cost low most of the time, but they need a live-though-minimally-sized version of the environment already running in the recovery Region so a failover only requires scaling it up, not launching a fully cold environment. Which DR strategy BEST matches this requirement?
options: Backup and restore, since restoring from an AWS Backup vault into a brand-new recovery Region environment is fastest when nothing is already running there.

Pilot light, which keeps only core data replicated and minimal core infrastructure like a database in the recovery Region, requiring the rest of the environment to be built and started at failover time.
Warm standby, which keeps a minimally sized but fully functional running copy of the environment in the recovery Region, scaled up to full capacity during a failover.
Multi-site active-active, which runs full production capacity in both Regions simultaneously at all times.
explanation: Warm standby keeps a scaled-down but fully functional copy of the whole application already running, so failover is a scale-up operation rather than a full build, matching the requirement for a minimally sized environment that's already live and an RTO of hours. Backup and restore has the lowest cost but the longest RTO, typically many hours to days, since almost nothing runs until restore begins. Pilot light keeps only core data and a minimal core (such as a database) ready, but the rest of the application stack, including compute, still needs to be provisioned at failover time, which is slower than scaling an already-running environment. Multi-site active-active runs full capacity in both Regions continuously, which costs far more than the low-cost requirement calls for.

stem: A company runs a fleet of on-premises and EC2 servers and wants continuous, block-level replication of those servers to a low-cost staging area in AWS, so that during a disaster they can launch fully booted recovery instances within minutes, matching the source servers' OS and applications, without pre-provisioning full-sized standby servers. Which AWS service BEST fits this requirement?
options: AWS Backup, taking a nightly backup of each server's root volume and restoring a new instance from the latest backup during a disaster.
AWS Application Migration Service configured for a one-time cutover migration with no ongoing replication.
Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager, scheduling EBS snapshots of each server's volumes every hour.
AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (AWS DRS), which continuously replicates source servers at the block level into a low-cost staging area and launches full recovery instances on failover.
explanation: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery continuously replicates source servers, on-premises or in AWS, at the block level into a low-cost staging area, and it launches fully provisioned recovery instances within minutes of a failover, which is exactly the pattern of a low-cost standby with a fast recovery. Nightly backups leave up to a day of data loss and a slower manual restore-and-boot process instead of minutes. Application Migration Service and DRS share underlying technology, but a one-time cutover migration is a different use case from an ongoing DR posture with continuous replication. Hourly EBS snapshots protect volume data but do not provide an automated, fast way to boot a full replacement server during a disaster.

stem: A CloudOps team wants to proactively validate, in a controlled experiment, that their application keeps serving traffic correctly if an Availability Zone's EC2 instances suddenly lose power, rather than waiting to discover this during a real outage. Which AWS service is purpose-built to safely run this kind of controlled fault-injection experiment?
options: AWS Config, by writing a custom rule that reports which resources exist in each Availability Zone.
Amazon Inspector, by scheduling a vulnerability scan targeted at the Availability Zone's instances.

AWS Fault Injection Service (FIS), which runs a defined experiment template that injects a fault, such as stopping instances in one Availability Zone, while enforcing stop conditions to limit blast radius.
AWS Trusted Advisor, by reviewing its fault-tolerance check results for the affected Availability Zone.
explanation: AWS Fault Injection Service runs defined experiment templates that inject real faults, like stopping instances in an Availability Zone, under guardrail stop conditions that halt the experiment automatically if things go wrong, purpose-built for controlled resiliency testing. AWS Config only reports resource configuration and inventory; it cannot inject a fault. Amazon Inspector scans for vulnerabilities, not resiliency behavior under fault conditions. Trusted Advisor's fault-tolerance check is a passive, point-in-time configuration review; it does not run any active experiment.

stem: A media company stores render assets on Amazon EFS and needs a second, independently usable copy of the file system in another AWS Region that stays continuously up to date, so the team can mount it and resume work quickly if the primary Region becomes unavailable. Which approach BEST meets this requirement?
options: Schedule a nightly AWS DataSync task that copies the entire file system to S3 and restores it to a new EFS file system only after a disaster is declared.
Enable EFS lifecycle management to transition infrequently accessed files to EFS Infrequent Access storage class.
Mount the same EFS file system directly from EC2 instances in a second Region over a VPC peering connection.
Enable EFS replication to a destination file system in a second Region, which continuously and automatically copies changes from the source file system.
explanation: EFS replication continuously and automatically copies changes to a destination file system in another Region, keeping it nearly current and ready to be promoted for use during a disaster. A nightly DataSync-to-S3-and-restore approach leaves up to a day of data loss and adds a manual restore step that is slower than promoting an already-replicating destination. EFS lifecycle management only changes the storage class for cost savings within the same file system; it does not create a Regional copy. EFS is a Regional service, so an EC2 instance in a second Region cannot mount the same file system directly across Regions with the low latency and independent availability this requirement needs.

stem: A platform team manages 40 AWS accounts under AWS Organizations and wants to deploy and keep in sync the same CloudFormation stack, a baseline security-monitoring stack, across all 40 accounts and three Regions each, with new accounts automatically receiving the stack as they join an organizational unit. Which TWO statements about using CloudFormation StackSets for this requirement are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: StackSets can only deploy a stack to a single account at a time, requiring the platform team to run 120 separate deployments by hand.
A stack instance created by a StackSet cannot be updated after creation; the underlying stack must be deleted and manually recreated for every template change.
Service-managed permissions integrate with AWS Organizations so a StackSet can automatically deploy to every account in a target organizational unit, including accounts added later.
StackSets requires every target account to pre-create the exact same IAM execution role by hand before any deployment can succeed, even with service-managed permissions.
A single StackSet operation can target multiple accounts and multiple Regions at once, and it tracks each resulting stack as a stack instance so the fleet can be updated or drift-detected centrally.
explanation: With service-managed permissions, a StackSet integrates with AWS Organizations and can target an organizational unit directly, automatically deploying to accounts added to it later. A single StackSet operation spans many accounts and Regions, and every resulting stack is tracked as a stack instance, so the whole fleet can be updated or drift-detected from one place. StackSets is built to avoid one-at-a-time manual deployments, not require them. Stack instances can be updated in place by updating the StackSet, with no delete-and-recreate cycle needed. Service-managed permissions specifically remove the need to pre-create a matching IAM role in every target account; that manual role setup is only required under the older self-managed permissions model.

stem: A team suspects that engineers have been making manual changes directly in the AWS Management Console to resources originally created by a CloudFormation stack, which risks the next stack update failing or silently reverting those changes. Which CloudFormation capability lets the team detect exactly which resources and properties have drifted from the stack's template definition, without performing an update?
options: Run CloudFormation drift detection on the stack, which compares each resource's actual configuration to the template and reports which resources and properties are DRIFTED, along with the differences.
Enable CloudFormation StackSets and let it silently re-apply the template to all target accounts on a fixed schedule.
Delete and recreate the stack from the same template so all resources are guaranteed to match the definition again.
Enable AWS Config recording for the stack's resources and wait for a weekly summary email.
explanation: CloudFormation drift detection compares each resource's live configuration against the stack's template and reports which resources and specific properties have drifted, with no update performed. StackSets manages multi-account, multi-Region deployment; it does not detect or report drift on its own. Deleting and recreating the stack is destructive and would cause an outage; it is not a detection mechanism. AWS Config records configuration history for compliance rules generally, but it is not the CloudFormation-native mechanism that compares a stack's live resources against its own template.

stem: Before applying an update to a production CloudFormation stack that changes an RDS instance's engine version and an Auto Scaling group's launch template, the team wants to see exactly which resources will be modified, replaced, or deleted, and confirm none of those changes will cause an unexpected resource replacement, before the update actually runs. Which CloudFormation feature BEST supports this review?
options: Stack policies, which permanently block updates to specific resource types.
A change set, which computes and previews the specific changes CloudFormation will make, including any resource replacements, before the update is executed.
Nested stacks, which split a template into smaller reusable templates.
The stack's rollback configuration, which defines CloudWatch alarms that trigger an automatic rollback after an update starts.
explanation: A change set computes and displays the exact actions CloudFormation will take, including which resources will be modified, replaced, or deleted, before anything is applied, letting the team catch an unexpected replacement in advance. A stack policy restricts which updates are allowed on specific resources; it does not preview an upcoming update's effects. Nested stacks are a template organization technique, not a change-preview mechanism. Rollback configuration only reacts after an update has already started, using alarms to trigger a rollback; it does not preview changes beforehand.

stem: An operations engineer needs to run an ad hoc command, restarting a specific service, across 200 EC2 instances tagged Environment=prod right now, without opening any inbound SSH or RDP ports and without pre-installing a bastion host. Which Systems Manager capability BEST fits this need?
options: AWS Config, targeting the same tag and remediating with a custom Lambda function.
Systems Manager Patch Manager, scheduling a patch baseline scan against the tagged instances.
Systems Manager Run Command, targeting instances by the Environment=prod tag and running a command document to restart the service, using the SSM Agent instead of SSH or RDP.
Systems Manager Session Manager, opening one interactive shell session per instance and typing the restart command 200 times.
explanation: Systems Manager Run Command targets managed instances by tag and executes a command document across the whole fleet at once through the SSM Agent, with no inbound ports or bastion host needed. AWS Config evaluates and records resource configuration; it is not built for on-demand command execution across a fleet. Patch Manager is scoped to patch scanning and installation, not arbitrary ad hoc commands like restarting a specific service. Session Manager could open a shell per instance, but doing that 200 times manually is far less efficient than a single Run Command execution targeted by tag.

stem: A CloudOps team must patch several hundred EC2 instances against the latest security updates every month, during a defined maintenance window, only applying patches that are already approved after a testing delay, and producing a compliance report showing which instances are missing an approved patch. Which TWO statements about using Systems Manager Patch Manager for this requirement are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: A patch baseline defines which patches are approved for installation, including an auto-approval delay so newly released patches are only applied after they have been available for a set number of days.
Patch Manager can only run against instances located in the same Region as the Patch Manager configuration itself, never across Regions in one operation.
Maintenance windows are unrelated to Patch Manager and can only be used to schedule Systems Manager Run Command executions, never patch scans or installs.
Patch Manager's compliance reporting shows, per instance, which approved patches are missing, letting the team confirm patch compliance without manually checking each instance.
Once a patch baseline is created, every instance in the account is automatically enrolled in it with no way to assign different baselines to different groups of instances.
explanation: A patch baseline defines the approval rules, including an auto-approval delay that holds back newly released patches for a set testing period, and Patch Manager's compliance reporting shows exactly which approved patches are missing on each instance. Patch Manager operations can span multiple Regions, not just the one the configuration lives in. Maintenance windows schedule Patch Manager scan-and-install tasks directly, alongside Run Command and other supported task types; they are not limited to Run Command only. Different patch groups, defined by a tag, can be assigned different baselines, so instances are not forced into one baseline account-wide.

stem: A company's security policy prohibits opening inbound port 22 on any EC2 instance's security group, but engineers still occasionally need an interactive shell on an instance for troubleshooting, with a full record of the session kept for audit. Which approach BEST satisfies both requirements?
options: Open port 22 only from the corporate VPN's IP range, and rely on the security group's flow logs for an audit trail.
Deploy a bastion host with port 22 open only from the bastion's own security group.
Configure an SSH key pair per instance and share the private key with the operations team over email.
Use Systems Manager Session Manager, which opens an interactive shell over the SSM Agent with no inbound ports required, and can log every session's commands and output to CloudWatch Logs or S3.
explanation: Systems Manager Session Manager opens an interactive shell through the SSM Agent with no inbound port required at all, and it can stream every session's activity to CloudWatch Logs or S3 for a full audit trail. Opening port 22 to the VPN range still leaves an inbound port open, which the policy prohibits, and flow logs only show connection metadata, not session content. A bastion host still requires an inbound port 22 somewhere in the path. Emailing a shared private key is also a security risk and provides no built-in session logging.

stem: An application running on multiple EC2 instances and Lambda functions needs a shared database connection string and a handful of feature-flag values, which change occasionally, without redeploying code, and with a version history the application can use to know the current value. Which AWS capability BEST fits this need at the lowest operational overhead?
options: AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store, storing each value as a parameter, using the standard tier for a handful of low-volume values and giving a version history the application can read through the SDK or API.
A static configuration file baked into a new AMI, requiring a rebuild and redeploy for every value change.
Environment variables set inside every server's user-data script, updated manually one instance at a time.
Amazon S3 with server-side encryption storing a single shared JSON file, downloaded manually before every deployment.
explanation: Systems Manager Parameter Store stores shared configuration values centrally, with the standard tier free for typical low-volume use, and it keeps a version history the application can query at runtime with no redeploy needed. Baking values into an AMI requires a full rebuild and redeploy for any change, which is exactly the overhead the requirement rules out. Updating user-data on every server manually does not scale and provides no centralized source of truth. Manually downloading a shared S3 file before each deployment adds a manual step and lacks the built-in versioning Parameter Store provides.

stem: A CloudOps team wants every managed EC2 instance in a fleet to continuously keep a specific antivirus agent installed and running, and to automatically reapply that configuration on a schedule if an instance drifts from it, without an engineer manually re-running an install script whenever an instance is found out of compliance. Which Systems Manager capability BEST fits this need?
options: Systems Manager Run Command, executed manually by an engineer whenever a compliance report shows an instance out of compliance.
Systems Manager State Manager, which defines an association that applies and re-applies a specified configuration document on a recurring schedule to keep managed instances in the desired state.
Systems Manager Patch Manager, scheduled to scan for missing OS patches only.
Systems Manager Parameter Store, storing the desired antivirus version number as a parameter for reference.
explanation: Systems Manager State Manager associations apply a configuration document on a recurring schedule and automatically reapply it if an instance drifts from the desired state, removing the need for manual re-runs. Run Command executed manually is exactly the manual re-run the team wants to eliminate. Patch Manager is scoped to OS and application patch compliance, not arbitrary software installation and enforcement like an antivirus agent. Parameter Store can hold a reference value, such as a version number, but it has no mechanism to enforce or reapply configuration on instances.

stem: A team currently uses an EC2 Auto Scaling launch configuration to define instance specifications for a group, but launch configurations cannot be modified once created and lack support for multiple instance types or newer EC2 features. The team wants a mechanism with versioning, so they can change the AMI or instance type and roll new versions out to the Auto Scaling group in a controlled way. Which approach BEST meets this need?
options: Continue creating a brand-new launch configuration and manually swapping it into the Auto Scaling group for every change.
Configure the Auto Scaling group to launch instances directly from a single hardcoded AMI ID, bypassing both launch configurations and launch templates.
Migrate the Auto Scaling group to use a launch template, which supports multiple numbered versions, so the group can reference a specific version or the latest or default version as it changes.
Store the instance specification in an AWS Config conformance pack and have Auto Scaling read from it directly.
explanation: An EC2 launch template supports multiple numbered versions, letting the team change the AMI or instance type in a new version while the Auto Scaling group references a specific version or tracks the latest or a designated default, giving controlled, versioned rollout. Continuing with launch configurations keeps the exact limitation the team wants to move away from, since each change still requires creating and swapping a whole new configuration. Hardcoding a single AMI ID with no template or configuration removes any structured way to manage or version instance specifications. AWS Config conformance packs evaluate compliance; Auto Scaling does not read launch specifications from them.

stem: A company builds a hardened, patched, standard Amazon Linux AMI that includes a specific runtime and security agent, and currently does this by manually launching an instance, installing software by hand, and creating an AMI from it every month. They want the build, test, and Region-distribution steps to run automatically on a defined schedule, with the same repeatable steps every time. Which AWS service BEST replaces this manual process?
options: AWS Systems Manager Automation, using a single generic runbook with no defined image-building components or testing stage.
Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager, since it also manages EBS snapshot schedules and can be reused for AMI builds.
AWS CodeDeploy, configured to install software onto an already-running fleet of instances.
EC2 Image Builder, which defines a repeatable pipeline of build components, test components, and Region distribution settings, and runs on a schedule to produce a new hardened AMI automatically.
explanation: EC2 Image Builder is purpose-built for exactly this: a pipeline of build components, test components, and distribution settings that runs on a schedule to produce a consistent, hardened AMI with no manual steps. Generic Systems Manager Automation runbooks are not structured around image build, test, and distribution stages the way an Image Builder pipeline is. Data Lifecycle Manager automates EBS snapshot and AMI lifecycle policies for existing resources; it does not build or customize a new AMI's contents. CodeDeploy installs application revisions onto already-running instances; it does not create AMIs.

stem: A platform team wants to let application teams self-service-provision a pre-approved, standardized set of resources, such as a three-tier web application stack, from a menu, without granting each application team direct IAM permissions to create the underlying EC2, RDS, and VPC resources themselves, and while still enforcing which CloudFormation template versions are allowed. Which AWS service BEST meets this need?
options: AWS Service Catalog, which lets the platform team publish approved CloudFormation-based products into a portfolio and grants only launch permissions to application teams, without granting direct resource-creation permissions.
AWS CloudFormation StackSets, granting every application team account administrator permissions to create their own stacks from a shared template.
AWS Config conformance packs, which evaluate resources for compliance after they are already created.
AWS Organizations service control policies (SCPs) alone, which can only deny actions and cannot provision any resources.
explanation: AWS Service Catalog publishes vetted CloudFormation-based products into a portfolio and grants application teams only permission to launch a product, not to create the underlying resources directly, satisfying both the self-service and governance requirements. Granting account administrator permissions so teams can run StackSets themselves defeats the purpose of restricting direct resource-creation access. AWS Config conformance packs check compliance after resources exist; they don't provide a self-service provisioning menu. SCPs can only restrict what IAM principals are allowed to do; they cannot provision anything themselves.

stem: A team deploys a new application version to an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer and wants zero-downtime deployments where the new version is fully launched and verified healthy on a completely separate set of instances before any production traffic is shifted to it, with the ability to shift traffic back to the original instances immediately if a problem is detected. Which AWS CodeDeploy deployment type BEST meets this requirement?
options: An in-place deployment, which stops the application on each existing instance, installs the new version, and restarts it, instance by instance.

A blue/green deployment, which provisions a replacement set of instances running the new version and reroutes load balancer traffic to them only after they pass health checks, keeping the original instances available for rollback.
A canary deployment defined entirely inside Amazon CloudFront, shifting a percentage of viewer requests to a second origin.
A rolling update performed directly by the Auto Scaling group's instance refresh feature, with no involvement from CodeDeploy.
explanation: A blue/green deployment in CodeDeploy provisions a full replacement set of instances, validates them, and only then shifts load balancer traffic, while keeping the original (blue) instances intact and ready for an immediate rollback. An in-place deployment reuses the existing instances, taking each one out of service briefly during the update, which does not give a fully separate, pre-verified fleet before any traffic shifts. CloudFront origin shifting is unrelated to CodeDeploy's EC2/On-Premises deployment model. Auto Scaling instance refresh performs a rolling replacement directly and is a different mechanism from a CodeDeploy blue/green deployment, without the same CodeDeploy-managed traffic-shifting and rollback controls.

stem: A team runs a web application on AWS Elastic Beanstalk and needs a deployment policy that avoids any reduction in the number of instances serving traffic during a new application version rollout, and that keeps the previous, known-good version's environment available to fail back to immediately if the new version fails health checks after traffic switches. Which Elastic Beanstalk deployment policy BEST meets this requirement?
options: All at once, which updates every instance in the environment simultaneously.
Rolling, which updates instances in batches within the existing environment, briefly taking each batch out of service.

Immutable, which launches a full set of new instances in a temporary Auto Scaling group running the new version, and only shifts traffic to them after they pass health checks, leaving the original environment untouched until the switch.
Rolling with additional batch, which launches one extra batch of new instances before beginning a normal rolling update.
explanation: The Immutable deployment policy launches an entirely new, full-capacity set of instances alongside the existing environment and only shifts traffic once they pass health checks, so serving capacity never drops and the original environment remains available to fail back to. All at once updates every existing instance simultaneously, causing downtime. Rolling takes each batch out of service temporarily, briefly reducing capacity, which the requirement rules out. Rolling with an additional batch reduces, but does not eliminate, that same temporary capacity dip during the update.

stem: A CloudOps team manages hundreds of EC2 instances across several teams and needs a queryable, centralized view of which operating system versions, installed applications, and network configurations exist across the fleet today, refreshed automatically, without connecting to every instance individually or maintaining a separate spreadsheet. Which Systems Manager capability BEST meets this need?
options: Systems Manager Session Manager, connecting to each instance interactively to run manual inventory commands.
Systems Manager Patch Manager, which only reports missing security patches, not general software or configuration inventory.
Systems Manager Parameter Store, storing a manually updated list of each instance's software as a parameter.
Systems Manager Inventory, which collects metadata such as installed applications, OS version, and network configuration from managed instances on a schedule and makes it queryable centrally.
explanation: Systems Manager Inventory automatically collects and centralizes metadata, including installed applications, OS version, and network configuration, from every managed instance on a recurring schedule, and it is queryable without touching any instance directly. Session Manager provides interactive shell access, not automated, centralized data collection across a fleet. Patch Manager is scoped to patch compliance, not general software or configuration inventory. Parameter Store only holds whatever values are manually written to it; it has no built-in fleet-wide collection capability.

stem: A developer's IAM user can list objects in an S3 bucket but receives Access Denied when trying to download a specific object, even though the user's own IAM policy grants s3:GetObject across the bucket's entire object path. Which is the MOST likely explanation, and how should the team confirm it?
options: The bucket's own bucket policy or the object's ACL contains an explicit deny or fails to grant the required permission for this principal; use the IAM Policy Simulator or inspect the bucket policy and object ACL directly to confirm.
IAM user policies are always the final word on S3 access, so no other policy could possibly block a request that an attached IAM policy allows.
The object must have been deleted, since Access Denied always means the object no longer exists.
S3 requires MFA for every GetObject call by default, and no configuration can change this.
explanation: Amazon S3 access is the combined result of the identity-based policy AND any resource-based bucket policy or ACL; an explicit deny anywhere, or a bucket policy that fails to also grant the permission, produces Access Denied even when the IAM policy allows the action. Checking the bucket policy and ACL, or running the request through the IAM Policy Simulator, is the standard way to find the blocking statement. IAM policies are only one input to the overall evaluation; a bucket policy or ACL can still restrict access. Access Denied is the standard response for a permissions problem, not a signal that the object was deleted (that would be a 404 Not Found). S3 does not require MFA for every GetObject call by default; that would require an explicit MFA condition in a policy.

stem: A CloudOps team wants to continuously check every new and existing S3 bucket for whether server-side encryption is enabled, and automatically enable default encryption on any bucket found without it, with no engineer manually reviewing each finding. Which combination of AWS Config capabilities BEST meets this need?
options: An AWS Config aggregator, which only combines compliance data from multiple accounts into a single read-only view.

An AWS Config managed rule that evaluates S3 bucket encryption, paired with an automatic remediation action using an SSM Automation document that enables default encryption on any NON_COMPLIANT bucket.
AWS Config resource inventory alone, which lists bucket configuration history but takes no corrective action.
A manually triggered AWS Config rule evaluation, run by an engineer once a quarter.
explanation: An AWS Config managed rule continuously evaluates bucket encryption, and attaching an automatic remediation action lets Config invoke an SSM Automation document to fix any NON_COMPLIANT bucket with no engineer involved. An aggregator only centralizes visibility across accounts; it does not evaluate or fix anything itself. Resource inventory tracks configuration history for reference; it has no remediation capability. A manual quarterly review is exactly the manual, delayed process the team wants to eliminate.

stem: A company wants to package a standard set of 15 related AWS Config rules and their remediation actions, covering a specific compliance framework, into a single deployable unit that can be applied consistently across many accounts in an AWS Organizations organization, rather than creating each of the 15 rules by hand in every account. Which AWS Config capability BEST meets this need?
options: AWS Config recorder settings, which control which resource types are tracked but do not bundle multiple rules together.
An AWS Config aggregator, which centralizes compliance visibility across accounts but does not deploy rules to them.
A conformance pack, deployed as a single template containing many Config rules and remediation actions, which can be deployed organization-wide through AWS Organizations.
AWS Config's resource relationship diagram, which only visualizes dependencies between existing resources.
explanation: A conformance pack bundles many Config rules and their remediation actions into one deployable template, and it can be deployed across an entire AWS Organizations organization in a single operation, avoiding rule-by-rule setup in every account. Recorder settings only control which resource types Config tracks, not which rules run. An aggregator is read-only visibility across accounts; it cannot push rules or remediations out to them. The resource relationship diagram is a visualization feature for existing resource dependencies, unrelated to packaging or deploying rules.

stem: A company wants to guarantee that no IAM principal in any member account of an Organizational Unit can ever disable AWS CloudTrail or delete its S3 log bucket, even if a member account's own administrator explicitly grants that permission through an IAM policy. Which AWS capability BEST enforces this account-wide, override-proof guardrail?
options: An IAM permissions boundary attached to every individual IAM role and user across every member account.
An AWS Config rule that only reports the CloudTrail configuration as noncompliant after the fact.
A resource-based bucket policy on the log bucket, which member account administrators are still able to modify or remove.

A Service Control Policy (SCP) attached to the Organizational Unit that explicitly denies the CloudTrail-stopping and bucket-deletion actions; SCPs set the maximum available permissions and cannot be overridden by any IAM policy within the account.
explanation: A Service Control Policy attached at the Organizational Unit level sets the ceiling of what any IAM principal in every member account can do, and an explicit deny in an SCP cannot be overridden by even a permissive IAM policy or an account administrator inside that account. A permissions boundary must be attached to each individual role or user and can be changed or removed by an administrator with sufficient IAM permissions in that account, so it is not an unbypassable, account-wide guardrail. An AWS Config rule only detects and reports a problem after it happens; it does not prevent the action. A bucket policy is also just a resource-based IAM policy that an account administrator with sufficient permissions can still modify or delete.

stem: A security team wants to ensure a KMS customer managed key used to encrypt sensitive data automatically generates new cryptographic material every year with no application changes or manual key swap, while ciphertext created under earlier key material remains decryptable. Which KMS capability BEST meets this need?
options: Automatic key rotation on the KMS customer managed key, which rotates the underlying key material yearly while keeping the same key ID and ARN, so existing ciphertext and applications continue to work unchanged.
Manually creating a brand-new KMS key every year and updating every application's configuration to reference the new key ARN.
Enabling S3 default encryption with SSE-S3, which uses Amazon-managed keys that the security team cannot configure a custom rotation schedule for.
Deleting and recreating the KMS key's alias annually, which generates entirely new key material under the same alias name.
explanation: Automatic key rotation on a KMS customer managed key rotates the backing key material on a yearly cadence while the key ID and ARN stay the same, so applications and existing ciphertext keep working with no code change or manual swap. Manually creating a new key every year requires updating every application's key reference and re-encrypting or managing multiple key versions by hand. SSE-S3 uses AWS-owned/managed keys with no customer-configurable rotation control, which does not meet a requirement for managing rotation on a customer managed key. Recreating an alias does not rotate key material; an alias is just a friendly pointer to a key, and deleting the underlying key would make old ciphertext unrecoverable.

stem: An RDS database credential is stored as a plaintext value in application configuration today, and the security team wants it rotated automatically on a schedule, with the new credential value pushed to the secret store and the database updated in the same operation, without the application ever handling the old credential directly in code. Which AWS service BEST fits this requirement?
options: AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store SecureString parameters, which do not include a built-in automatic rotation workflow for database credentials.
AWS Secrets Manager, which supports scheduled automatic rotation using a Lambda rotation function that updates both the secret value and the database credential together.
AWS KMS, which only encrypts and decrypts data and does not store or rotate credential values itself.
Hardcoding the credential in the application's environment variables and redeploying manually every 90 days.
explanation: AWS Secrets Manager supports scheduled automatic rotation through a Lambda rotation function that changes the database credential and updates the stored secret value together, with no manual step. Parameter Store SecureString parameters store an encrypted value but have no built-in rotation workflow for database credentials the way Secrets Manager does. KMS only performs encryption and decryption operations; it does not store secrets or manage their rotation. Hardcoding the credential and redeploying manually every 90 days is a manual process that also briefly exposes the credential in code and deployment artifacts.

stem: A security team wants continuous, managed threat detection that analyzes VPC Flow Logs, DNS query logs, and CloudTrail events to identify things like a compromised EC2 instance communicating with a known malicious IP address, without deploying any agents on EC2 instances. Which AWS service BEST meets this requirement?
options: AWS Config, evaluating resource configuration for compliance drift.
Amazon Inspector, scanning EC2 instances and container images for software vulnerabilities.
Amazon GuardDuty, which continuously analyzes VPC Flow Logs, DNS logs, and CloudTrail events using threat intelligence to generate findings, with no agent required.
AWS Trusted Advisor, reviewing weekly security checks in the console.
explanation: Amazon GuardDuty is a managed, agentless threat detection service that continuously analyzes VPC Flow Logs, DNS logs, and CloudTrail events against threat intelligence to surface findings like communication with a known malicious IP. AWS Config evaluates resource configuration for compliance, not network or API threat behavior. Amazon Inspector scans for software and container vulnerabilities, a different problem from detecting active threat behavior. Trusted Advisor's security checks are a periodic best-practice review, not continuous threat detection.

stem: A company runs GuardDuty, Inspector, and Config across a dozen accounts and wants a single, aggregated dashboard that shows security findings from all three services together, checks resources against standards like the AWS Foundational Security Best Practices, and produces an overall security score, instead of an engineer checking each service's console separately in every account. Which AWS service BEST meets this need?
options: Amazon Macie, which only classifies and discovers sensitive data in S3.
AWS Config aggregators, which centralize only Config rule compliance data, not findings from GuardDuty or Inspector.
AWS Organizations, which manages account structure and billing but has no built-in security-findings dashboard.

AWS Security Hub, which aggregates and normalizes findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, Config, and other services into one dashboard, evaluates resources against security standards, and produces an overall security score.
explanation: AWS Security Hub is purpose-built to aggregate and normalize findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, Config, and other integrated services into a single view, run standards checks such as the AWS Foundational Security Best Practices, and compute a security score. Macie only covers sensitive-data discovery in S3; it does not aggregate findings from other security services. A Config aggregator only centralizes Config rule compliance, leaving GuardDuty and Inspector findings out of the picture. AWS Organizations manages account and billing structure, not security findings.

stem: A company operates 25 AWS accounts under AWS Organizations and needs a tamper-evident audit record of every API call made in every account and Region, centrally stored, with a way to cryptographically prove after the fact that none of the stored log files have been altered or deleted. Which TWO statements about meeting this requirement with AWS CloudTrail are correct? (Select TWO.)
options: A single-Region CloudTrail trail in each account automatically captures API activity from every Region without any additional configuration.
